So for a small open economy, taxing imports will almost always be suboptimal. And because a small country take world prices as a given, any tax on imported goods simply drives a wedge between the international price and the domestic price without improving the country's terms of trade. So this distortion results in an unambiguous welfare reduction because prices to domestic consumers increase and consumers and first substitute away from the efficient foreign suppliers and production shifts towards less efficient domestic alternatives. Import tax is also violent the core optimal tax principle of production efficiency since they effectively tax intermediate inputs and risk costs throughout the economy. And unlike broad-based consumption taxes such as VAT, import taxes or tariffs narrow the tax base and create avoidable deadweight loss. So with no market power to shift the burden abroad, a small and open economy ends up bearing the full cost of the distortion while gaining none of the strategic or welfare benefits that might justify such a policy for a larger economy. And we We welcome the thoughts about providing optionality for the taxpayer, but nevertheless, we think that it's important that in our discussions going forward, we also look into these wider effects to see, ensure that we deliver solutions that can in fact support domestic resource mobilisation. Thank you very much, Chair. Sierra Leone aligns with the position of the African Group. As Protocol 1 should preserve flexibility for source states in choosing the appropriate method of taxation for cross-border services while ensuring balanced allocation of taxing rights between source and residence jurisdiction. CILoN believes that the protocol should not impose a single mandatory method, but instead recognize methods already widely used by developing countries and reflected in tax treaty practice. CILoN emphasized that tax treaties traditionally limit the extent of source state taxation, but do not prescribe the method by which such taxation should be exercised. Accordingly, CILM supports that protocol one should explicitly recognize that source states may tax cross-border services either on a gross basis, withholding tax, or on a net basis, provided that any agreed rate limits or caps are expected. Avoid language that implicitly favors net basis taxation, which often requires complex profit attribution, permanent establishment determinations, and transfer pricing analysis. This flexibility is essential for developing countries whose administrative capacities and access to information may not support effective net basis taxation in all cases. Sierra Leone, in line with the African group, support the gross basis withholding approach as a primary and practical method for taxing cross-border services. This approach is justified because it is simpler to administer and enforce, particularly where the service provider has no physical presence. It aligns with the existing domestic laws and treaty practice in many African countries. It ensures early and secure revenue collection, reducing compliance risks and base erosion. The protocol should therefore recognize gross basis withholding as a legitimate and effective method, especially for digital, remote, and highly mobile services. Allow states to rely on withholding mechanisms without being required to demonstrate net profits or economic substance. CILON supports the African group position that different categories of services may justify different tax treatment and rates. The protocol should allow states to apply differentiated retailing tax rates depending on the nature of the service, such as technical management and consultancy services, digital and automated services, highly specialized or capital light services, reflect variations in profit margins, mobility, and ease of tax planning across service types. This flexibility is critical to prevent based erosion through service recharacterization. allow states to design tax system consistent with domestic economic reality and development priorities. Such an approach promotes fairness, administrative feasibility, and sustainable revenue mobilization for developing countries in a globalized digital economy. Thank you, Madam Chair.

Thank you very much for that comprehensive input. That was very helpful. Thank you. We have stakeholder one, which is the Committee of Fiscal Studies, not Affairs, so I stand to be corrected there. Please go ahead.

Thank you for the opportunity, Madam Khalid. As many delegates have highlighted, the net income option would be the fairest approach to sharing rights to tax between the country of location of the supplier of the services and that of the client or the customer. Succession of net income would require a global approach due to the mismatches between where the expenditures are born and where the revenues derive. This has been recognized in the work on pillar one in the G20 OECD project on base erosion and profit shifting. The draft multilateral convention for amount A actually provides a detailed methodology that could be applied to determine the global consolidated net income adjusted for tax purposes and for allocating an agreed share to countries where the sales take place based on specific sourcing rules, which also take account of the importance of data from users of digital services. While this may seem to be an ambitious objective, it should be part of the agenda for this work stream, especially building on the blocks that have been largely agreed under Pillar One. It has also been pointed out in the discussion that while withholding taxes on gross income offer a practical short-term solution, they do not resolve the fundamental flaws of the international tax system, are unrelated to profitability, and can easily be passed on to customers. Determining an appropriate withholding tax rate is also problematic, as a uniform rate is unsuitable given the highly variated nature of services. Many automated digital services have very high marginal profit rates, while those for labor-intensive professional services are much lower. However, differential rates could create categorization problems and pose significant administrative challenges. A possible option, and again, this has been discussed here today, could be the approach that combines the alternatives for withholding taxes on gross payments and taxation of net income based on some form of apportionment. This could be designed along the lines of Article 12AA, as you mentioned, Madame Kholid, or 12B of the UN model, which includes the option of a simple apportionment method applying the multinational enterprises global profit rate to local revenues. However, the withholding tax rate would need to be high enough for the net income option to be effective in practice. Alternatively, a specified percentage of gross income could be treated as the minimum payable. In our view, the optimal solution remains the comprehensive approach adopted for amount of pillar one as the only effective way to ensure the allocation of rights to tax the net income among countries where real activities take place. This could be applied to the bulk of services that are either automated or digitally deliverable, perhaps with limited exclusions or specific alternatives. for particular categories of services. I thank you.
